CT extends deadline to get gift cards to ex-SNAP beneficiaries

by Keith M. Phaneuf, CT Mirror
November 16, 2026

Gov. Ned Lamont’s administration is giving thousands of former federal nutrition assistance beneficiaries an extra month to claim the $300 grocery store gift cards first pledged to them in early June.

Department of Social Services spokeswoman Christine Stuart confirmed Monday the administration has extended its self-imposed deadline from Nov. 30 to Dec. 31 to get cards to an estimated 25,000 former recipients of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits.

The department, which is working with regional nonprofit community action agencies, will send another round of text messages to eligible residents in hopes of disbursing as much relief as possible.

“Residents are advised to visit their local community action agency, show ID, and get their card on the spot,” the department wrote in a memo to state legislators about the deadline extension.

A full list of action agencies and their contact information is available on the Connecticut Association for Community Action website.

“I hope residents are able to take advantage of it,” said Sen. Matt Lesser, D-Middletown, co-chairman of the Human Services Committee and one of the lawmakers who pressed Lamont to intensify Connecticut’s response to federal human services cutbacks. “I know that the demand is significant.”

Lamont has faced increasing pressure to intervene since July 2025, when Congress and President Donald Trump ordered major cutbacks to SNAP and other federal human services programs.

Veterans, people experiencing homelessness, former foster youths and parents with children older than 14 all face tougher work requirements. Many lawfully present immigrants, including refugees, lost eligibility. And critics say tougher error penalties from Washington have led states to unfairly disqualify many SNAP applicants.

The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a fiscal policy group based in Washington, D.C., reported in mid-October that SNAP enrollment is at its lowest point nationwide in 17 years. Connecticut Voices for Children, a local policy and research organization, noted in August that nearly 63,000 Connecticut residents, including almost 19,000 children, had lost federal nutrition benefits since July 2025.

Lamont has invested millions of state dollars in Connecticut Foodshare, a nonprofit that supports hundreds of food pantries, shelters, community kitchens and other community-based assistance programs.

But anti-hunger advocates say food pantries and related programs can mitigate only a fraction of the problem created when households lose access to SNAP benefits.

The governor, who recently was reelected to a third term, announced on June 3 he would use state surplus funds to send $7.5 million, in the form of $300 grocery store gift cards, to 25,000 former SNAP recipients.

Distribution was set to begin Aug. 4, but the administration has struggled to get relief to eligible residents.

As of Oct. 27, aid had been provided to about 2,000 of the 25,000 residents, only about 8%. The social services department announced at that time it would streamline efforts to process claims for cards. And while it had used text messages and postcards last summer and fall to notify those eligible, another round of texting is planned.

We just set a new bar by winning the Pulitzer Prize for Local Reporting.   The award is a crowning achievement sitting atop a mountain of substantive impact, including change spurred by the On the Hook series that was recognized. It woke up public officials to the festering practice of towing and quickly selling people’s cars before their owners could hope to get them back. The story immediately changed the law that allowed it to happen (as immediate as government can move). That’s what you get from CT Mirror: high caliber, high impact journalism.   The newsroom didn’t begin their multi-year investigation into the towing industry with a thought that it would win them a Pulitzer, but they did know they had something momentous that could reshape public policy.  For every long-term investigation that didn’t win a Pulitzer, many still could have for the level of reporting we did and the changes in lives and laws that came from them. He has been the state finances reporter at CT Mirror since it launched in 2010. Prior to joining CT Mirror Keith was State Capitol bureau chief for The Journal Inquirer of Manchester, a reporter for the Day of New London, and a former contributing writer to The New York Times.
